mainTopic: Confirming a husband's death: certain-death cases, miracles in the great pit, and trusting overheard talk and a גוי's casual report
overview: This amud continues the discussion of when we may accept that a missing husband has died, so his wife can remarry. It first finishes a disagreement about a man who fell among snakes and scorpions. Then it brings a ברייתא about a man who fell into a furnace or a boiling cauldron. Next it discusses רבי מאיר's story of a man who survived three days in the great pit. The חכמים answer that we do not learn from miracles, and the גמרא explains that staying awake for three days is the miracle. A related story tells how the daughter of נחוניא חופר שיחין was saved from the same pit, and how ה׳ judges the righteous very strictly. A new משנה then allows even overheard talk of women or children to count, and it trusts a גוי only when he speaks casually (מסיח לפי תומו). Through stories of reports about חיואי, a horseman, and חסא who drowned, the גמרא teaches that a wife whose husband fell into מים שאין להם סוף may not remarry from the start, but stays married if she already did. A final story about a גוי's boast continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The worry that he may be a snake charmer
steps.stepSummary: The opinion that does not allow testimony gives its reason: maybe the man is a חבר, a charmer who can keep snakes and scorpions from hurting him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps he is a charmer.
steps.whatsHappening: The text opens in the middle of a disagreement about a man who fell into a pit full of snakes and scorpions. The opinion that does not let witnesses testify that he died gives its reason: maybe he is a snake charmer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Falling among snakes and scorpions normally means certain death. This opinion worries about an unusual person, a חבר, who knows how to control such creatures, so his death cannot be assumed.

keyTerms.meaning: A charmer, someone with a special skill or spell to control snakes and scorpions
We may testify about him that he died

phrases.english: Perhaps he is a charmer.
phrases.notes: This goes back to the man who fell into a pit of snakes and scorpions.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the explanation of the snakes-and-scorpions case from before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not testify about him, because he might be a charmer who can control snakes.

steps.title: Why the first opinion is not worried about charmers
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא allows testimony because even a charmer gets hurt when he crashes down on top of the snakes.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the תנא קמא holds: because of the pressure, they will harm him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the תנא קמא does not share the worry about a charmer. When the man lands on the snakes with force, they will bite him anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא does not deny that charmers exist. His point is that a charm does not help when you suddenly fall and crush the creatures, because pressed and frightened snakes will strike. So death can still be assumed.

keyTerms.meaning: The first (unnamed) opinion in a teaching
Because of, as a result of

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree a charmer can normally control snakes. They argue about whether the force of falling on them cancels that protection.

phrases.english: And the first Tanna (why does he allow testimony?):
Because of the pressure, they harm him.
phrases.notes: The man's body landing on the snakes squeezes them, so they bite even a charmer.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא קַמָּא, אַגַּב אִיצְצָא מַזְּקִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the unspoken question of why the תנא קמא ignores the charmer worry raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the other side's reasoning by narrowing the worry: a charm does not work under crushing pressure.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think a charmer is always safe from snakes, so his death can never be assumed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Under the force of a fall the snakes harm even a charmer, so testimony is allowed.

steps.title: Falling into a furnace or a boiling cauldron
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that witnesses may testify about a man who fell into a burning furnace, or into a boiling cauldron of wine or oil.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If he fell into a fiery furnace, we testify about him. Into a cauldron full of wine or oil, we testify about him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with two more cases where death is certain enough to testify: a burning furnace and a boiling cauldron of wine or oil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cases count as certain death, so the wife may remarry based on this testimony. This first opinion treats wine and oil the same, which sets up רבי אחא's distinction in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A large cooking pot or cauldron over a fire

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: נָפַל לְתוֹךְ כִּבְשַׁן הָאֵשׁ — מְעִידִין עָלָיו.
phrases.english: If he fell into a fiery furnace, we may testify about him (that he died).

phrases.aramaic: לְיוֹרָה מְלֵאָה יַיִן וָשֶׁמֶן — מְעִידִין עָלָיו.
phrases.english: Into a cauldron full of wine or oil, we may testify about him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: נָפַל לְתוֹךְ כִּבְשַׁן הָאֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the snakes case to new cases of certain death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who fell into a fiery furnace, or into a boiling cauldron of wine or oil, may be declared dead by witnesses.

steps.title: רבי אחא: oil is fatal, wine might not be
steps.stepSummary: In רבי אחא's name they distinguish: with oil we testify because it feeds the fire, but with wine we do not, because it puts the fire out.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the name of רבי אחא they said: Of oil, we testify about him, because it ignites. Of wine, we do not testify about him, because it extinguishes.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion splits the cauldron case into two. A cauldron of oil counts as certain death, but a cauldron of wine does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the man falls in, liquid splashes onto the fire below. Oil makes the fire stronger, so the heat rises. Wine puts the fire out, so he might survive and testimony is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Ignites, makes the fire burn stronger

phrases.english: In the name of Rabbi Acha they said:
A cauldron of oil: we may testify about him,
because it ignites (the fire).
A cauldron of wine: we may not testify about him,
because it extinguishes (the fire).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with step 3 about the wine cauldron.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oil cauldron: testify. Wine cauldron: do not testify, because the spilled wine may put out the fire.

steps.title: The answer: wine feeds the fire in the end
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים answer רבי אחא that wine puts out the fire only at first, but afterward it makes the fire burn stronger, so the wine case is also certain death.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: At first it extinguishes, but in the end it ignites.
steps.whatsHappening: The other חכמים push back on רבי אחא's distinction. They agree wine dampens the fire at first, but say it later makes the fire stronger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This undoes רבי אחא's reason for treating wine differently. Since the fire ends up hotter either way, the man in the wine cauldron is also assumed dead. This brings us back to the first opinion in step 3.

keyTerms.meaning: They said to him (a reply from other חכמים)

steps.whatToRemember: The final position treats both wine and oil cauldrons as certain death: wine only dampens the fire for a moment and then makes it stronger.

phrases.english: They said to him:
At first it extinguishes, and in the end it ignites.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: תְּחִלָּתוֹ מְכַבֶּה וְסוֹפוֹ מַבְעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reasoning of רבי אחא in step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבי אחא's claim that wine saves the man by putting out the fire.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He only looked at the first effect of the wine. In the end the wine makes the fire burn stronger.

steps.title: Quoting רבי מאיר's story from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה where רבי מאיר tells of a man who fell into the great pit and came out alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר said: There was an incident with someone who fell into the great pit, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to quote a line from the משנה. This sets up the next discussion: רבי מאיר told a story about a man who fell into a huge pit and survived.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי מאיר uses this story to argue that falling into a pit of water is not always certain death. The וכו׳ tells us the rest of the story is in the משנה: the man came up after three days.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a real event used as evidence
Etc.; the rest is quoted from the source

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir said:

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאֶחָד שֶׁנָּפַל לַבּוֹר הַגָּדוֹל וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: There was an incident with one who fell into the great pit, etc.
phrases.notes: In the משנה the story ends with him coming up alive after three days.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאֶחָד שֶׁנָּפַל לַבּוֹר הַגָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר brings a story of a man who survived three days in a great pit.

steps.title: The חכמים: we do not learn from miracles
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records that the חכמים answered רבי מאיר that we do not bring miraculous events as proof for הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: They said to רבי מאיר: We do not mention miraculous events.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא shows the response to רבי מאיר's story. The חכמים say it was a miracle, and miracles cannot set a general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים do not deny the story happened. They say a miracle is an exception, so it tells us nothing about what normally happens to someone who falls into a pit. This pushes the גמרא to ask what exactly was miraculous.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
We do not mention or bring as proof

steps.whyThisMatters: This is an important rule for learning הלכה: a one-time miracle cannot be used as proof for what normally happens.

phrases.english: It was taught: They said to Rabbi Meir:
We do not mention miraculous events.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמְרוּ לוֹ לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר: אֵין מַזְכִּירִין מַעֲשֵׂה נִסִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof רבי מאיר brought in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's use of the great pit story as proof.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The man's survival was a miracle, and a miracle cannot teach us what normally happens.

steps.title: What was the miracle?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which part of the story made it miraculous.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the miraculous event?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question: what exactly about this man's survival was a miracle? This sets up the attempts to answer in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply surviving a fall into water is not obviously a miracle. The גמרא needs to find the part of the story that goes beyond nature.

phrases.english: What is the miraculous event?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the חכמים's claim in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which part of the great pit story was beyond nature.

steps.title: Not eating or drinking is not a miracle
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the miracle was going three days without food or drink, then rejects this from the פסוק in מגילת אסתר, where people fasted three days.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it was that he did not eat or drink, but it is written: 'Fast for me and do not eat and do not drink.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one answer: maybe the miracle was surviving three days without food or drink. It immediately pushes back with a פסוק showing people can fast three days naturally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אסתר asked the Jews to fast for three days, without eating or drinking. Since a natural, required fast lasted that long, surviving three days without food is not a miracle, so this cannot be the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a suggestion that will be rejected)
But isn't it written? (a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: If you say it was that he did not eat and did not drink,
but isn't it written:
"And fast for me, and do not eat and do not drink."
phrases.notes: אסתר 4:16. The פסוק goes on to say "three days," which is the point here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to step 8 and rejects it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that going without food and drink for three days was the miracle.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק shows people fasted three days and survived naturally, so this is not miraculous.

steps.title: The miracle was going without sleep
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the miracle was that the man did not sleep for three days.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it was that he did not sleep.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real answer: the miracle was staying awake for three days. If he had fallen asleep in the pit, he would have drowned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food and water can be missed for three days, but sleep cannot. The next step brings a source showing that going three days without sleep is impossible.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the miracle was surviving without food. The גמרא just ruled that out. The miracle is staying awake.

phrases.english: Rather, it was that he did not sleep.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines which part of the story was the miracle.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The miracle was surviving without food and drink.
steps.terutzMaskana: The miracle was staying awake for three days.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: no one can stay awake three days
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports this with רבי יוחנן's ruling: someone who swears not to sleep for three days gets lashes for a false oath and may sleep right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יוחנן said: An oath that I will not sleep for three days, they give him lashes, and he sleeps immediately.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that going three days without sleep is impossible. רבי יוחנן treats an oath not to sleep for three days as a שבועת שוא, an oath that is empty because it cannot be kept.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because no person can keep such an oath, it is a vain oath from the start. He receives מלקות for it, and the oath does not bind him, so he may sleep immediately. This shows that staying awake three days in the pit must have been a miracle, which supports the חכמים's answer to רבי מאיר.
steps.whatToRemember: The חכמים reject רבי מאיר's story because the man stayed awake three days, which is impossible by nature (רבי יוחנן). A miracle cannot teach a general הלכה.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yochanan said:
(If one says:) "An oath that I will not sleep for three days,"
they give him lashes, and he may sleep immediately.
phrases.notes: He gets lashes because swearing to do something impossible is an empty oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אִישַׁן שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings proof for the answer in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that staying awake three days is beyond nature, which makes the story miraculous.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's ruling that an oath not to sleep for three days is a vain oath, punished with lashes, and he may sleep right away.

steps.title: What is רבי מאיר's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי מאיר did not consider the man's three days without sleep a miracle.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מאיר, what is his reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now knows that the miracle was going three days without sleep. It asks how רבי מאיר can say this was not a miracle, which sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 11, רבי יוחנן ruled that a person cannot go three days without sleep. So if the man stayed awake that long, it seems to be a real miracle. The גמרא wants to know how רבי מאיר explains it naturally.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא who told the great pit story to show that a man who falls into water may survive, so his wife may not remarry

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir, what is the reason?
phrases.notes: He means: why didn't רבי מאיר see this as a miracle, if no one can go three days without sleep?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from Step 11, which proved that staying awake three days would be a miracle.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How רבי מאיר explains the man's survival without a miracle.

steps.title: There were arches inside the cistern
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא explains that the cistern had layers of arches, so the man could lean on them and sleep.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: There were arches on top of arches.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא answers the question: the Great Cistern was built with rows of arches stacked one above another. The man could have rested on them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there was something to hold onto, the man did not have to stay awake the whole time. He could sleep while leaning on the arches. So, according to רבי מאיר, nothing impossible happened.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who explains רבי מאיר

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
There were arches on top of arches.
phrases.notes: So the man in the cistern had something to lean on while he slept.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא כִּיפִּין עַל גַּב כִּיפִּין הֲווֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The arches inside the cistern let the man rest and sleep, so his survival was natural.

steps.title: The חכמים say the arches were marble
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים hold that the arches were smooth marble, so the man could not hold on and sleep.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים: they were made of marble.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the חכמים still call it a miracle. The arches were made of slippery marble, so he could not rest on them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that there were arches. They disagree about whether a person could really hold onto them. For the חכמים, smooth marble means no grip and no sleep, so it stays a miracle.

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים who argue with רבי מאיר

phrases.english: And the Rabbis: they were of marble.
phrases.notes: Marble is smooth, so you can't grab onto it and fall asleep.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the חכמים' reason for rejecting the explanation of Step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the arches made sleep possible.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Marble arches are too slippery to hold onto while sleeping.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: he must have dozed a little
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר holds that, even on marble, the man surely grabbed hold for a moment and slept a bit.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מאיר: it is impossible that he did not cling on and sleep a little.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר answers the חכמים. Even if the arches were marble, the man surely managed to hold on and doze for short moments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר does not need long, full sleep. A few short naps are enough to survive three days. So for him the case is still natural, and we may rely on it for הלכה.
steps.whatToRemember: The whole argument is about the facts: רבי מאיר says the man could doze while holding the arches, so it was natural; the חכמים say marble made that impossible, so it was a miracle, and we don't learn הלכה from miracles.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir:
it is impossible that he did not cling on
and sleep a little.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי מֵאִיר אִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּלָא מְסָרֵיךְ וְנָיֵים פּוּרְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי מאיר's response to the חכמים' marble argument in Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual reasoning: short naps are enough to explain the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Marble arches make any sleep impossible, so it must be a miracle.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even on marble a person manages to hold on briefly and doze, so it is not a miracle.

steps.title: נחוניא's daughter falls into the Great Cistern
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how נחוניא חופר שיחין's daughter fell into the Great Cistern, and רבי חנינא בן דוסא reported hour by hour that she was safe and then that she had come up.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: There was a story with the daughter of נחוניא the well digger, who fell into the Great Cistern. People came and told רבי חנינא בן דוסא. In the first hour he told them: She is safe. In the second hour he said: She is safe. In the third hour he said: She has come up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story about another person who fell into the same Great Cistern. רבי חנינא בן דוסא calmly tells the people she is safe, and later that she is out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The link to the sugya is the בור הגדול, the same cistern from the earlier case. Here the girl really was saved in an unusual way. The next step explains how רבי חנינא בן דוסא knew.

keyTerms.meaning: נחוניא the digger of water pits, who dug wells for the public
A תנא famous for his righteousness and powerful prayer

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּבִתּוֹ שֶׁל נְחוּנְיָא חוֹפֵר שִׁיחִין
phrases.english: An incident with the daughter of Nechunya the well digger
who fell into the Great Cistern,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָאוּ וְהוֹדִיעוּ לְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא.
phrases.english: and they came and told Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa.
In the first hour, he said to them: Peace.
phrases.notes: "Peace" here means she is safe and unharmed.

phrases.english: In the second, he said to them: Peace.
In the third, he said to them: She has come up.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן מַעֲשֶׂה בְּבִתּוֹ שֶׁל נְחוּנְיָא חוֹפֵר שִׁיחִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related story about the same Great Cistern mentioned in the discussion of the arches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נחוניא's daughter fell into the Great Cistern and was saved, as רבי חנינא בן דוסא foretold.

steps.title: How she was saved, and how רבי חנינא בן דוסא knew
steps.stepSummary: The girl says a ram led by an old man pulled her up. רבי חנינא בן דוסא says he is no prophet; he simply knew a righteous man's children would not be harmed by his own good work.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: My daughter, who brought you up? She said to him: A ram came by me, and an old man was leading it. They said to him: Are you a prophet? He said to them: "I am not a prophet, and I am not the son of a prophet." Rather, could it be that the very thing a righteous man works at would make his children stumble?
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: the girl explains how she was rescued. Then people ask רבי חנינא בן דוסא how he knew, and he explains his reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נחוניא spent his life digging water pits for the public. רבי חנינא בן דוסא reasoned that ה׳ would not let his child die through that very project. So his knowledge came from trust in the merit of a צדיק, not from prophecy.

phrases.english: He said to her: My daughter, who brought you up?

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרָה לוֹ: זָכָר שֶׁל רְחֵלִים נִזְדַּמֵּן לִי,
phrases.english: She said to him: A male sheep came by me,
and an old man was leading it.
They said to him: Are you a prophet?
He said to them: "I am not a prophet,
phrases.notes: עמוס 7:14

phrases.english: and I am not the son of a prophet,"
rather: the thing that the righteous man is busy with,
phrases.notes: The righteous man is נחוניא, and the thing he works at is digging water pits for people.

phrases.english: should his children stumble through it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of Step 16 and explains how רבי חנינא בן דוסא knew she would be saved.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The merit of a righteous person's good work protects his children from harm through that same work.

steps.title: רבי אבא: Yet נחוניא's son died of thirst
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא says that, despite this, נחוניא's son died of thirst, because ה׳ is exacting with the righteous to a hair's width.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said: Even so, his son died of thirst, as it says: "And around Him it storms greatly." This teaches that הקדוש ברוך הוא is exacting with those around Him like a hair's width.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא adds a sad twist to the story. Even though נחוניא dealt with water for the public, his own son died of thirst.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 taught that a צדיק's merit protects his children. רבי אבא shows this protection has limits: ה׳ judges the righteous very strictly, even for tiny faults. He reads the word נשערה as connected to שערה, a hair.

keyTerms.meaning: Those around Him, the righteous who are close to ה׳
Like a strand of hair, extremely precise

steps.confusionAlert: This does not contradict the story about the daughter. The daughter was saved through her father's merit, but רבי אבא teaches that even a צדיק's family is judged very strictly, so his son still died.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי כֵן מֵת בְּנוֹ בַּצָּמָא,
phrases.english: Even so, his son died of thirst,
phrases.notes: This is נחוניא's son, even though his father spent his life providing water.

phrases.english: as it says: "And around Him it storms greatly,"
phrases.notes: תהלים 50:3. The word נשערה sounds like שערה, a hair.

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְדַקְדֵּק עִם סְבִיבָיו
phrases.english: which teaches that the Holy One, Blessed be He, is exacting with those around Him
like a strand of hair.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אַף עַל פִּי כֵן מֵת בְּנוֹ בַּצָּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the idea of Step 17 that a צדיק's merit protects his children.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ judges the righteous extremely strictly, as learned from תהלים 50:3.

steps.title: רבי חנינא learns the same idea from a different פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא brings another פסוק showing that ה׳ is most feared by those closest to Him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said, from here: "A God feared in the great council of the holy ones, and awesome over all who are around Him."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא agrees with the idea that ה׳ is very strict with the righteous. He just learns it from a different פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ה׳ is feared most "over all who are around Him." Those closest to Him, the righteous, have the most reason to fear, because He judges them most strictly. This supports רבי אבא's point about נחוניא's son.

keyTerms.meaning: The council of the holy ones

steps.whatToRemember: The closer a person is to ה׳, the more strictly he is judged. נחוניא's merit saved his daughter, yet his son still died of thirst.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said, from here:
"A God feared in the great council of the holy ones,
phrases.notes: תהלים 89:8

phrases.english: and awesome over all who are around Him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different פסוק for the same idea רבי אבא taught in Step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ is most feared by, and most exacting with, those who are closest to Him (תהלים 89:8).

steps.title: Even overheard talk of women or children is enough
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that hearing women say a man died is enough, and רבי יהודה says even children talking about going to bury him is enough, whether or not the speaker means to testify.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Even if someone heard women saying "So-and-so died," that is enough. רבי יהודה says: even if he heard children saying "We are going to eulogize and bury so-and-so." This works whether the speaker means to testify or does not mean to.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It teaches that even very weak sources, like women's talk or children's talk, are enough to confirm a man died so his wife can remarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally women and children cannot be formal witnesses. Here the rules are relaxed, since we only need to know the husband died so his wife may remarry. The speaker's intent does not matter: casual talk counts just as much as a deliberate statement.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה, the main text being studied
To eulogize, to give a funeral speech
Means to, intends (here: intends to testify)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a full court testimony. The rules are relaxed only for confirming a husband's death so his wife may remarry.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how far חכמים went to avoid leaving a woman unable to remarry.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
Even if he heard from the women
saying: "So-and-so died"
— it is enough for him.
phrases.notes: He means it's enough for this person to testify, so the wife may remarry.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה says:
Even if he heard from the children saying
"We are going to eulogize
and to bury so-and-so."
Whether he intends to testify,
or whether he does not intend to.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the story section about נחוניא חופר שיחין ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Overheard talk from women, and according to רבי יהודה even children, is enough to confirm a death, whether or not the speaker means to testify.

steps.title: A Jew may testify on purpose, a non-Jew only casually
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בבא says a Jew is believed even if he means to testify, but a non-Jew who means to testify is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בבא says: a Jew is believed even if he intends to testify. But a non-Jew, if he intended to testify, his testimony is not testimony.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה בן בבא adds a split: a Jew is believed either way, but a non-Jew is believed only when he is not trying to testify.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A non-Jew who sets out to testify might have a reason to shade the truth. When he just mentions the death in passing, with no aim, we trust it. A Jew is trusted even when he speaks as a witness.
steps.whatToRemember: A non-Jew's words count only when said casually, not as deliberate testimony.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה בן בבא says:

phrases.aramaic: בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא מִתְכַּוֵּין,
phrases.english: With a Jew, even though he intends to testify, he is believed;
but with a non-Jew, if he intended to testify
— his testimony is not valid testimony.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a distinction to the intent rule just stated in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Jew is believed even when intending to testify; a non-Jew is believed only when not intending to testify.

steps.title: Maybe the children never went
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if children only say they are going to a funeral, maybe they will not actually go.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: But maybe they will not go?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's case of the children. Saying "we are going" does not prove the man really died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Children talking about a future funeral may just be guessing that a sick man will die. Maybe he recovers and no funeral ever happens. So their words seem too weak to rely on.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
But perhaps they will not go?
phrases.notes: The worry: maybe the children only expected him to die, and in the end he didn't.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of רבי יהודה's case in the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's ruling relying on children saying "we are going to bury so-and-so"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A statement about a future funeral does not prove the death happened; the plan may never happen.

steps.title: The children say they are coming back from the burial
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the children are speaking about a burial they already came back from.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: it is where they say, "We are coming from eulogizing and burying so-and-so."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is really about children talking in the past tense, coming home from the funeral.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the burial already happened, there is no doubt about whether they will go. This fixes the problem by changing the case from future plans to a past event.

phrases.english: רב יהודה said that שמואל said:
It is where they say: "We are coming
from eulogizing and from burying so-and-so."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל דְּקָאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the children not going.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (past tense instead of future)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The children were talking about a funeral that had not yet happened.
steps.terutzMaskana: The children are reporting a burial they already came back from.

steps.title: Maybe they buried a grasshopper
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: maybe the children only buried a dead grasshopper and called it by the man's name as a game.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe just a grasshopper died for them, and they brought it out for burial calling it by his name!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again: children play games, so even a past-tense "burial" might be pretend.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Children may hold a play funeral for a bug and give it a person's name. Then their words would tell us nothing about the real man. So even the past-tense version still seems unreliable.

phrases.english: But perhaps merely a grasshopper of theirs died
and they brought it out for burial under his name!
phrases.notes: "His name" means the name of the man we're asking about. The kids might be playing pretend.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer just given in שמואל's name.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's case of children coming back from a burial
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Children may have held a pretend funeral for an insect named after the man, so their report proves nothing.

steps.title: The children name the rabbis and eulogizers who were there
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the children give real details: which rabbis and which eulogizers were at the funeral.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is where they say: such and such rabbis were there; such and such eulogizers were there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is where the children mention specific rabbis and eulogizers at the funeral.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Real rabbis and professional eulogizers do not attend a grasshopper's play funeral. These details show the children describe a real burial of the man. So their words can be trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: Eulogizers, people who give funeral speeches

steps.whatToRemember: Children's report of a death counts when it is about a past burial and includes real details like who was there.

phrases.english: It is where they say:
Such and such rabbis were there.
Such and such eulogizers were there.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּקָאָמְרִי כֵּן וְכֵן רַבָּנַן הֲווֹ הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the grasshopper challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding details to the case that rule out a game
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The children's funeral might have been a pretend burial of an insect.
steps.terutzMaskana: The children name real rabbis and eulogizers who attended, proving a real funeral took place.

steps.title: שמואל narrows the rule about a non-Jew who means to testify
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting שמואל, says the משנה only rejects a גוי who means to permit the woman to remarry. A גוי who only means to report the death is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And with a גוי, if he intended to testify, his testimony is not testimony.' רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: This only applies when he intended to permit her to remarry. But if he only intended to testify about the death, his testimony counts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a גוי who 'intends' to testify. Then שמואל explains that the rule is narrower than it looks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל splits 'intending' into two kinds. Intending להתיר, to get the woman permitted to remarry, makes the גוי unreliable. Intending להעיד, just to report a fact, does not disqualify him.

keyTerms.meaning: He has an intention or purpose
To testify (just to report a fact)
'They only taught this when…'; it limits a rule to a narrower case

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two intentions. 'To permit' (asking the court to let her remarry) is bad, while 'to testify' (only reporting the death) is fine according to שמואל.

phrases.english: And with a non-Jew, if he was intending, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה, whose full line ends: 'his testimony is not testimony.'

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
They only taught this where he intended to permit her,
but if he intended to testify,
his testimony is valid testimony.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's rule about a גוי (step 21) after the side discussion about children.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גוי who intends to get the woman permitted is not believed. A גוי who only intends to report the death is believed.

steps.title: How can we tell what the non-Jew intended?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how a court can know which kind of intention the גוי had.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know which one he intended?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about שמואל's rule. This sets up רב יוסף's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Intention is inside a person's head. If the הלכה depends on it, we need an outside sign that shows which kind of intention he had.

phrases.english: How do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how שמואל's distinction can be used in practice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A test that tells 'intending to permit' apart from 'intending to testify'.

steps.title: רב יוסף: it depends on what he asks the court
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says the difference shows in his words. If he says 'let his wife marry,' he means to permit. If he only says 'he died,' he means to testify.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: If he came to the court and said, 'So-and-so died, let his wife marry,' he intends to permit. If he simply said 'He died,' he intends to testify.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers the question by pointing to the גוי's exact words in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Asking the court to let the wife marry shows that he wants a certain result, so he is not trusted. Just stating the fact of the death shows no such goal, so his words count as testimony according to שמואל.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
If he came to the court and said:
'So-and-so died, let his wife marry,'
this is intending to permit.
If he simply said 'He died,'
this is intending to testify.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: בָּא לְבֵית דִּין וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Adding 'let his wife marry' shows intent to permit. Saying only 'he died' shows intent to testify.

steps.title: ריש לקיש says the same as שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reports that ריש לקיש also gave this same narrow reading of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also stated: ריש לקיש said: They only taught this when he intended to permit her. But if he intended to testify, his testimony counts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that another אמורא, ריש לקיש, held the same view as שמואל. This also sets up רבי יוחנן's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is added to the הלכה here. What it does add is that ריש לקיש in ארץ ישראל held this view as well, so now רבי יוחנן can respond to it.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated; another אמורא said the same

phrases.english: It was also stated:
Reish Lakish said:
They only taught this where he intended to permit her,
but if he intended to testify,
his testimony is valid testimony.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second אמורא who holds the same view as שמואל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Same as שמואל: only a גוי who intends to permit is not believed.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the Sages already rejected this view
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reminds ריש לקיש that אושעיא ברבי once said this exact thing to 85 elders, and the חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said to him: Wasn't there a story with אושעיא ברבי, who permitted women to remarry while he was with eighty-five elders? He told them: 'They only taught this when he intended to permit, but if he intended to testify, his testimony counts.' And the חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן challenges ריש לקיש with a past event. This exact idea was already put forward and turned down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not a logical argument but history. The majority of the חכמים already rejected the narrow reading. So a גוי who means to testify in any way is not believed.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident, a story that happened
אושעיא 'the great one', a leading early sage
They did not agree with him

steps.whyThisMatters: The הלכה follows the חכמים here: a גוי's deliberate report, even a simple 'he died', cannot be used to let the wife remarry.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said to him:
Wasn't there such an incident
with Oshaya the great one,
who permitted them, together with eighty-five elders?
phrases.notes: 'Them' means women whose husbands' deaths were reported by non-Jews.

phrases.english: He said to them:
They only taught this where he intended to permit her,
but if he intended to testify, his testimony is valid testimony.
And the Sages did not agree with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לֹא כָּךְ הָיָה מַעֲשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks ריש לקיש's (and שמואל's) narrow reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a גוי who only means to testify is believed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same view was raised by אושעיא ברבי in front of the חכמים, and they rejected it.

steps.title: Then when is a non-Jew ever believed?
steps.stepSummary: If even a simple report is not trusted, the גמרא asks what case the משנה could mean when it suggests that a גוי who does not intend to testify is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then the משנה, which teaches 'And with a גוי, if he intended, his testimony is not testimony,' where can you find a case where he is believed?
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting שמואל's reading, the גמרא asks what the משנה's words 'if he intended' can still mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה implies that some גוי who does not 'intend' is believed. If even a plain 'he died' said in court counts as intending, the גמרא needs to find a case where a גוי has no intention at all.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you find (such a case)?

phrases.english: But the משנה, which teaches:
'And with a non-Jew, if he was intending,
his testimony is not testimony,'
how can you find a case for it?
phrases.notes: He means the other side: a case where a non-Jew is believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from rejecting the narrow reading: now what does the משנה mean?
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's implied case of a believed גוי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If every report is called 'intending', the משנה's distinction seems to have no case left.

steps.title: Answer: when he speaks casually
steps.stepSummary: A גוי is believed only when he mentions the death casually, without trying to give testimony.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he speaks casually, without any purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the believed case is a גוי who just mentions the death in passing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מסיח לפי תומו means talking naturally, not aimed at a court or a result. Such talk has no motive behind it, so it is trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: Speaking casually, in innocence, without intending to testify

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה follows the חכמים: a גוי is believed about a husband's death only when he speaks casually (מסיח לפי תומו), not when he comes to testify.

phrases.english: When he speaks offhandedly, in innocence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines the case the משנה refers to
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No case seemed left where a גוי is believed.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is believed when he speaks casually, מסיח לפי תומו.

steps.title: Example: the man calling out about חיואי
steps.stepSummary: A גוי went around calling 'Who is from חיואי's family? חיואי died!', and רב יוסף let חיואי's wife remarry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like that man who was walking along saying: 'Who is from the house of חיואי? Who is from the house of חיואי? חיואי died!' And רב יוסף let his wife marry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real case of מסיח לפי תומו that was used to let a wife remarry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man was not standing in court or asking for a ruling. He was just calling out the news. That is casual talk, so רב יוסף relied on it.

keyTerms.meaning: He was saying as he went along

phrases.english: Like that man who was going along saying:
'Who is there from the house of Chivai,
who is there from the house of Chivai,
Chivai has died!'
And Rav Yosef let his wife marry.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rule of step 32 in practice.
steps.raayaObject: A casual report by a גוי is enough to let the wife remarry.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יוסף's ruling in the case of חיואי.

steps.title: Example: the brave horseman of פומבדיתא
steps.stepSummary: A גוי went around mourning 'the brave horseman of פומבדיתא who died', and רב יוסף (or רבא) let his wife remarry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another man was walking along saying: 'Woe for the brave horseman who was in פומבדיתא, who died!' And רב יוסף, and some say רבא, let his wife marry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second example of a casual report that was relied on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the man is just sighing over a death, not telling anyone what to do. That kind of natural talk is exactly מסיח לפי תומו.

phrases.english: There was a man who was going along saying:
'Woe for the brave horseman
who was in Pumbedita, for he has died!'
And Rav Yosef, and some say Rava, let
his wife marry.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּהֲוָה קָאָמַר וְאָזֵיל: וַוי לֵיהּ לְפָרָשָׁא זְרִיזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second example, alongside step 33.
steps.raayaObject: A casual report by a גוי is relied on.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling of רב יוסף (or רבא) about the horseman.

steps.title: The story of חסא who drowned
steps.stepSummary: A גוי called out that חסא had drowned. רב נחמן said 'the fish ate him', and because of that, חסא's wife remarried and nobody objected.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another man was walking along saying: 'Who is from the house of חסא? חסא drowned!' רב נחמן said: 'By God! The fish have eaten חסא.' Because of רב נחמן's words, חסא's wife went and married, and nobody said anything to her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a third story, this time about a drowning, which leads to a new הלכה in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן did not give a formal ruling. He only showed that he was sure חסא was dead. The wife remarried based on that, and nobody stopped her, which is the point רב אשי will learn from.

phrases.english: There was a man who was going along saying:
'Who is there from the house of Chasa? Chasa has drowned!'
Rav Nachman said: By God!
The fish have eaten Chasa.
Because of Rav Nachman's words,
Chasa's wife went and married,
and they did not say anything at all to her.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּהֲוָה קָאָמַר וְאָזֵיל: מַאן אִיכָּא בֵּי חָסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another casual-report story, which turns the discussion toward drowning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Based on רב נחמן's words, חסא's wife remarried and nobody objected.

steps.title: רב אשי: endless water forbids her only from the start
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי learns from חסא's story that the rule forbidding a wife whose husband fell into מים שאין להם סוף applies only לכתחילה. If she already married, she is not taken away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Learn from this that when the חכמים said 'If he fell into water with no visible end, his wife is forbidden,' that is only לכתחילה. But if someone already married her, we do not take her away from him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי draws a הלכה from what happened with חסא's wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a woman whose husband drowned in מים שאין להם סוף may not remarry, because he might have come out of the water somewhere out of sight. Since nobody objected after חסא's wife married, רב אשי concludes that this is only a rule for before the fact. After the fact, the marriage stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Water whose edges cannot be seen
We do not take her away (from her new husband)

steps.whatToRemember: A wife whose husband drowned in מים שאין להם סוף should not remarry לכתחילה. But if she already did, בדיעבד, she stays married.
steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not saying מים שאין להם סוף is allowed. It is still forbidden לכתחילה; only an already-done marriage is left alone.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Learn from this:
phrases.notes: He assumes חסא drowned in water whose edges could not be seen.

phrases.english: That which the Sages said,

phrases.aramaic: מַיִם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם סוֹף אִשְׁתּוֹ אֲסוּרָה,
phrases.english: 'endless water, his wife is forbidden,'
this applies only at the outset,
but if someone married her,
we do not take her away from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a הלכה from the story of חסא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ban on remarrying after the husband falls into מים שאין להם סוף is only לכתחילה. If she already remarried, she is not separated from her new husband.

steps.title: Second version: רב נחמן himself let חסא's wife remarry
steps.stepSummary: According to another version, רב נחמן actively permitted חסא's wife to remarry. His reason was that חסא was a famous man, so if he had survived, everyone would have heard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רב נחמן actually let חסא's wife remarry. He said: חסא is an important man. If he had come up out of the water alive, people would have heard about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of the חסא story from step 35. Here רב נחמן himself allows the wife to remarry, and he gives a specific reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 35, רב נחמן only said 'the fish ate him', and the wife remarried on her own. In this version, he actually rules that she may remarry. His reason is special to חסא: a great man's rescue would be public news, so silence means he died.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say; introduces a different version of a story or ruling
He married her off; he allowed her to marry
The matter would have publicity; people would hear about it

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. In step 35, רב נחמן just said 'the fish ate him' and the wife remarried on her own. Here he actively permits it.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Rav Nachman allowed his wife to marry,
phrases.notes: 'His wife' means חסא's wife, the woman from the story just before.

phrases.english: he said: Chasa is a great man;
if it were so that he came up out of the water,
the matter would have had publicity.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אַנְסְבַהּ רַב נַחְמָן לִדְבֵיתְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the חסא story. This version would undo רב אשי's lesson in step 36, because the remarriage was permitted from the start and only because חסא was famous.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן permitted חסא's wife to remarry because a great man's survival would have become known.

steps.title: Rejecting the 'great man' reasoning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the second version's reasoning. Whether or not the husband is famous, a wife whose husband fell into endless water may stay married after the fact but may not marry from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is not correct. It makes no difference whether he is a great man or not. After the fact, yes, she may stay married. From the start, no, she may not marry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the 'great man' reasoning of step 37. It returns to the rule רב אשי taught in step 36.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 37 suggested a special exception for famous people. The גמרא says fame does not change the law. The rule is the same for everyone: דיעבד she may stay married, לכתחילה she may not marry.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is not so; the גמרא rejects the previous idea
After the fact; once it already happened

steps.whatToRemember: For a husband who fell into מים שאין להם סוף, his fame does not matter. If his wife already remarried, she stays married. She may not remarry from the start.
steps.whyThisMatters: This confirms רב אשי's rule from step 36 as the final הלכה. It also blocks a 'famous person' exception.

phrases.english: But that is not so:
it is no different if he is a great man,
and no different if he is not a great man;
after the fact, yes; from the start, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reasoning of step 37 and restores the rule of step 36.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that a great man's fame makes the remarriage permitted from the start.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Fame makes no difference to the law. The rule of דיעבד yes, לכתחילה no applies to everyone.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For anyone who drowned in endless water, his wife may stay married after the fact but may not marry from the start.

steps.title: A non-Jew boasts that he killed a Jew, and the widow comes to אביי
steps.stepSummary: A גוי threatens a Jew to work for him on שבת. As part of the threat, he says he killed another Jew who refused to cook for him on שבת. The dead man's wife hears this and asks אביי if she may remarry.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain גוי said to a Jew: 'Cut the fodder and throw it to my animals on שבת. If you don't, I will kill you, just as I killed a certain Jew. I told him to cook me a pot on שבת, he didn't cook it, and I killed him.' That man's wife heard and came before אביי. He held off on ruling for her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story about a גוי who mentions killing a Jew while threatening someone else. This step sets up the case, and אביי's handling of it continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects to step 32: a גוי is believed only when he mentions a death casually, not as testimony. Here the גוי mentions the death in the middle of a threat, so the question is whether that counts as a casual mention. The word שהיתא shows that אביי did not rule right away.

keyTerms.meaning: He delayed her; he held off on ruling for her

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא גּוֹי דַּהֲוָה קָאָמַר לֵיהּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל:
phrases.english: There was a certain gentile who was saying to a Jew:
Cut down the fodder
and throw it to my animals on Shabbos,
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are added in the corrected wording, so read the word as 'my animals'.

phrases.english: and if not, I will kill you
just as I killed so-and-so the Jew,

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַרִי לֵיהּ: בַּשֵּׁיל לִי קְדֵירָה בְּשַׁבָּת,
phrases.english: for I said to him: Cook me a pot on Shabbos,
and he didn't cook for me, so I killed him.
His wife heard,
phrases.notes: This is the wife of the Jew the גוי said he killed.

phrases.english: and she came before Abaye.
He held her off.
phrases.notes: This word is in round brackets, so some versions have it and some don't. It means אביי delayed giving her an answer.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גּוֹי דַּהֲוָה קָאָמַר לֵיהּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the drowning cases to the theme of a גוי reporting a death. Here the report comes inside a threat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: a גוי's boast of killing a Jew, said in the middle of a threat, reaches the wife. אביי holds off on ruling, and the outcome comes next.
